Persia. The ancient and classical name for the vast empire and region centered on what is now modern-day Iran derives from the Achaemenid heartland in southwestern Iran. The nation officially adopted Iran, meaning land of the Aryans in Persian, as its official English name in nineteen-thirty-five under Reza Shah Pahlavi, though the change gained wider recognition and enforcement after the nineteen-seventy-nine Islamic Revolution. The shift reflected a desire to emphasize national identity rooted in Aryan heritage rather than European colonial nomenclature.

Throughout antiquity and into the modern era, the region was called Persia. Reza Shah Pahlavi formally requested all nations use Iran in international discourse beginning in nineteen-thirty-five, though adoption of the change was gradual outside the region. The Persian Empire under the Achaemenids, ruling from five-fifty to three-thirty BCE, was one of the ancient world's largest empires, encompassing three continents. Persian culture, language, and philosophy profoundly influenced Islamic civilization and extended into medieval European thought via Spain and the Crusades.

The nineteen-seventy-nine Islamic Revolution consolidated the identity shift, establishing the Islamic Republic of Iran and severing ties with the Pahlavi monarchy. The name Iran derives from Old Persian Aryanam, meaning realm of the Aryans, emphasizing indigenous heritage over colonial-era European terminology. Contemporary Iran straddles ancient Zoroastrian, Islamic, and secular identities, maintaining Persian as its lingua franca across ethnic minorities. The connections to the Achaemenid empire, the Sassanid empire, the Safavid empire which established Shia Islam as the state religion, and Zoroastrianism, the ancient Persian religion, all underscore the deep historical roots Iran reclaimed when it cast off the colonial name Persia.
